content: Systemic hypotension is a frequent complication in preterm infants and is associated with significant risks, including periventricular hemorrhage, white matter injury, and poor neurodevelopmental outcomes. Corticosteroids have been explored as a treatment option, either as a primary therapy or as an adjunct to conventional approaches such as volume expansion and vasopressor or inotropic therapy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of corticosteroids in treating hypotension in preterm infants, either as a first-line treatment or for cases of hypotension that are resistant to standard therapies. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving preterm infants (less than 37 weeks of gestation and under 28 days old) who were treated with corticosteroids. Studies comparing corticosteroids (administered orally or intravenously) to placebo, other cardiovascular support drugs, or no treatment were included. The methodological quality of the studies was assessed to minimize biases, including selection, performance, attrition, and detection biases. Data were analyzed using standard methods, with treatment effects expressed as relative risk, risk reduction, number needed to treat (NNT), and weighted mean difference, all with 95% confidence intervals. Four studies involving a total of 123 infants were included in the review. In one study, hydrocortisone was compared to dopamine as a primary treatment for hypotension. Persistent hypotension was more common in the hydrocortisone group compared to the dopamine group (relative risk [RR] 8.2, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.47 to 142.6; risk difference [RD] 0.19, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.37). However, in two studies comparing corticosteroids to placebo for refractory hypotension, persistent hypotension (defined as the continued need for inotropic support) was less common in the corticosteroid-treated group (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.65; RD -0.47, 95% CI -0.68 to -0.26; NNT = 2.1, 95% CI 1.47 to 3.8). No significant effects were observed on other shortor long-term outcomes. Two additional studies, currently available only in abstract form, may be eligible for inclusion in future updates of this review. The authors concluded that hydrocortisone may be as effective as dopamine when used as a primary treatment for hypotension in preterm infants. However, the long-term safety of hydrocortisone in this context remains unknown. Corticosteroids appear to be effective in treating refractory hypotension without an increase in short-term adverse effects. Nevertheless, due to the lack of long-term safety and benefit data, corticosteroids cannot be routinely recommended for the treatment of hypotension in preterm infants.
